From Middle English hil (“hill”), from Old English hyll (“hill”), from Proto-West Germanic *hulli (“hill”), from Proto-Germanic *hulliz (“hill”), from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”) (compare also Proto-Germanic *halluz (“stone, rock”)).

senses.d: An elevated landmass smaller than a mountain.
ex: The park is sheltered from the wind by a hill to the east.

Jack and Gill
Went up the hill,
To fetch a bottle of water.

senses.d: A sloping part of a landscape, especially one with a road, trail, etc.
ex: You need to pick up speed to get up the hill that's coming up.

senses.d: A heap of earth surrounding a plant.
A single cluster or group of plants growing close together, and having the earth heaped up about them.
ex: a hill of corn or potatoes

senses.d: The raised portion of the surface of a vinyl record.
To form into a heap or mound.
ex: Spread, heaped up, stacked with good things; and redolent of citrons and grapes, hilling round tall vases of wine;

senses.d: To heap or draw earth around plants.
ex: After the seeds were inserted, the earth was hilled up all around into a smooth little mound.
